topic: Mini Agent Gateway: Building Code That Constrains the LLM

key_points: Lightweight ReAct-style local LLM agent runtime with dynamic tool registry, multi-step reasoning, execution tracing, and runtime safety controls
Architecture: User Input -> Web UI/CLI -> agent.py -> prompts.py -> dispatcher.py -> schemas.py -> tools.json -> tools.py -> Tool Result -> ReAct loop
Single tools.json drives tool descriptions, validation schemas, and runtime tool registration simultaneously
Schema-based argument validation (schemas.py) and a tool normalization layer constrain what the LLM can call
OpenAI-compatible local LLM endpoint; works with vLLM, FastAPI, Ollama-style backends
Dual-layer architecture: LLM Gateway Proxy layer (multi-provider routing, rate limits, fallback, token accounting) + Agentic Harness layer (context assembly, tool execution, memory, safety checks)
Dynamic routing across Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o based on latency, cost, or capability
Zero client-side key exposure via full-stack proxy; API keys stay isolated on backend
Pre-execution guardrails: content sanitization, PII filtering, safety policy verification
Comparison matrix evaluates direct API integration vs LLM Gateway vs Full Agent Harness on latency, cost, statefulness, tool integration, governance
The LLM is the smallest part of an agent system; the harness (memory, tooling, routing, guardrails) does the real work
Agent harness provides structured execution environment: observation, context assembly, tool execution, memory retention, safety, iterative goal satisfaction
Production-grade agents require a production-grade data platform for state and memory
Claw Patrol (Show HN, ~112 points) positions as a security firewall for agents - policy enforcement between LLM and tools
Constrains agent tool calls through a security/guard layer, proving the gateway pattern for safety
Community traction indicates strong demand for agent-constraint tooling
Rayline routes Claude Code subagents to on-device and cheaper models (Show HN, ~11 points)
Cost/latency optimization by routing subagent traffic through a gateway
Practical example of a gateway that constrains WHICH model handles which call

stats.fact: Claw Patrol, an agent security firewall, drew ~112 points on Hacker News (2026), signaling high demand for tool-call constraint tooling.
Arch GW markets a distributed gateway for agents 'engineered with small LLMs', reflecting a trend toward routing agent traffic through cheaper/on-device models.

Enterprise reference architectures routinely pair a centralized LLM gateway (multi-provider routing, token accounting, rate limiting, fallback) with an agentic harness layer that manages context, tools, memory, and guardrails.
OpenAI-compatible local endpoints (vLLM, Ollama, FastAPI) are the standard interface for small self-hosted agent gateways, keeping model routing vendor-neutral.
MongoDB argues the agent harness, not the LLM, is the dominant component of production agent systems because it owns state, tooling, memory, and safety.

angles: Position the gateway/harness as the real engineering surface - the LLM is a pluggable component, not the system
Constraint as the core idea: schema validation, tool allow-lists, guardrails, and model routing are what make the LLM trustworthy
Cost + safety dual win: routing to cheaper/on-device models saves tokens while policy layers stop dangerous tool calls
Build-up approach: start with a ReAct loop + tools.json registry, then layer in validation, tracing, routing, and guardrails
Zero-secret-exposure proxy pattern for production deployments
Hands-on how-to framing with concrete code layers (prompts, schemas, dispatcher, tools) that beginners can copy
